newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch ATA to review lifeless wheat contract.
newsitem.headline: Dutch ATA to review lifeless wheat contract.

text.p: Lack of interest in trading wheat futures on Amsterdam's Agricultural Futures market (ATA) has prompted the exchange to go back and consult the industry on possible modifications only three months after the new contracts were launched.
"We're looking at reasons why the contract is not doing as well as expected," exchange spokesman Kasper Walet said.
"That involves speaking to people in the industry to find out what they think should be changed. We want to get a feeling about why they aren't using it."

So far, the Dutch contract has traded just 472 contracts, way below initial hopes. The ATA carefully avoided making any firm turnover predictions at the launch but volumes are clearly well below expectations.
Walet said the consultation process was an informal "sounding out" process involving potential contract users. It was too early to say if results would be officially published.
"Maybe we won't make any decision at all. The contract has been running for a couple of months, people are aware of it and it's just to get a idea of how they feel about it," he said.

The Europe-wide contract, designed for the continent's farmers producing bread-milling wheat, was launched in the Netherlands in early June at a time when speculative interest in the U.S. grain markets was high.

A race to set up a European contract had developed between the ATA and France's MATIF, with the Dutch exchange stealing a month's head start on its rival. The French plan, delayed by legal obstacles, was finally launched in early July.
But the rush to get a contract off the ground may have been part of the problem. The ATA has said the timing of its start, in between harvests, was to blame for lacklustre participation.

"Everybody seems happy with the specifications of the contract, that's not the problem," Walet said. "My own feeling is that people are waiting for someone else to start trading before committing themselves."
He added that in addition the physical market has also calmed since the summer's tight market condititions and this had fed through into futures activity, or lack of it.
"The MATIF is experiencing similar problems," he said.
The French contract has consistently traded below 100 lots a day, when industry estimates were targeting a daily 1,000-tonne volume within two years.

These teething problems are sure to be watched with interest by the London Commodity Exchange and the London Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), which have placed their own wheat contract high on the agenda after merging.
Germany is also looking to start a Hanover-based contract, but Walet said the choice of a new trading system there would probably mean there would not be a launch until 1998.
Although this could be in the German's favour.
"By the time we launch, hopefully we will have learned from the ATA's and MATIF's mistakes," Hanover exchange official Otto Kroeger said earlier this year.
